analysis.one_liner: Forgives a California farm water district's debts to federal taxpayers and hands it federally built water facilities.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 27-12, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law the 2015 settlement between the federal government and Westlands Water District, California's largest agricultural water district. It would erase the district's capital repayment obligations on federal water contracts, give it title to federally built canals, pumping plants, and offices, and lift long-standing federal reclamation law limits on land ownership and subsidized water pricing for the district's lands. In exchange, the district would take over legal responsibility for managing tainted farm drainage water within its own boundaries.
analysis.who_benefits: Growers in Westlands Water District — large farming operations on the west side of the San Joaquin Valley. They would be relieved of repaying federal construction costs going back to 1960s water contracts, receive title to federal facilities, and be exempt from reclamation law ownership limits and full-cost pricing requirements that apply to other federal water users.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large Westlands Water District farm operators

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Interior Department to carry out the September 15, 2015 settlement agreement between the United States and Westlands Water District that ended litigation over the government's unbuilt drainage system.

Upon executing a new repayment contract, the district would be relieved of its capital repayment obligations under its 1963 water service contract and its 1965 repayment contract with the United States.

Once its capital repayment obligation is discharged, the ownership limits and full-cost pricing rules of federal reclamation law would no longer apply to lands in the district — rules designed to keep federally subsidized water tied to family-sized farms.

The district would receive title to the San Luis Canal system (about 1,045 miles of buried pipeline), pumping plants, the Mendota Pool diversion facilities, the Pleasant Valley system, the drainage collection system, and two field offices.
Costs the United States incurred planning or studying drainage service for the district would be nonreimbursable — taxpayers absorb them.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would absorb the district's unrepaid capital obligations and the cost of planning the never-built drainage system, and who would permanently give up the district's repayment debt and the reclamation law pricing limits on its lands.

drawbacks.text: The district would assume full legal responsibility for managing drainage water within its boundaries and could not discharge drain water outside them — and Interior would have no duty to provide drainage service to the unit.
The district would have to indemnify the United States for claims arising from transferred facilities and finance any needed repairs — but only after taxpayers hand over the assets.
The relief would not cover operation and maintenance costs, future capital costs, or unallocated construction costs, and the district would still owe Restoration Fund charges.

Critics of the underlying settlement noted that drainage water in this valley carries selenium — the reason the federal drain was shut in the 1980s after wildlife damage at the Kesterson refuge — so leaving the district to manage it internally could mean contaminated water stays on or under farmland rather than being exported.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine trade: Westlands would take on a real liability (drainage water it cannot send anywhere else) and future costs, which is what the government got in the settlement. But the headline effect runs the other way: hundreds of millions of dollars in federal repayment debt erased, federally built infrastructure transferred, and the reclamation law limits on land ownership and subsidized pricing repealed for the district's lands. The bill's design concentrates its benefits on the district's largest landowners while the offsetting obligations are those the government already failed to meet for decades.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Natural Resources Committee, got a subcommittee hearing, and was approved in committee markup 27-12 — but it was never reported to the full House or brought to a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. David Valadao introduced the bill on January 12, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources; it had no cosponsors.
The Water, Power and Oceans subcommittee held a hearing on May 24, 2016.
The full committee held markups on November 15-16, 2016, discharged the subcommittee, and ordered the bill reported in amended form by a vote of 27-12.
No further action followed; the bill was never reported to the House or debated on the floor, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers keep the district's outstanding repayment obligations and the reclamation law ownership and pricing limits on its lands — but the decades-old drainage dispute also remains unresolved, with neither the district nor the government holding a final settlement.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors, yet the committee approved the bill 27-12, suggesting some bipartisan support in committee; the party split of that vote and of the floor scheduling decision is not in the record.

industries.industry: Large agricultural operations in Westlands Water District
industries.note: The bill would erase the district's capital repayment debts, transfer federally built canals and pumping plants to it, and repeal reclamation law ownership and full-cost pricing limits on its lands — the rules meant to keep federal water subsidies tied to family-sized farms. Its gain is taxpayers' loss of the repayment debt and permanent subsidy of large landholdings.
The bill expressly bars shifting the district's costs, water allocations, or Restoration Fund payments onto other federal water contractors, including hydropower preference contractors.

Taxpayers would absorb the district's unrepaid capital obligations and nonreimbursable drainage planning costs, and give up title to federally built infrastructure, in exchange for the district taking on drainage liability within its boundaries.
